newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish president Robinson not to seek a second term.
newsitem.headline: Irish president Robinson not to seek a second term.

text.p: Irish president Mary Robinson said on Wednesday she would not seek a second seven-year term of office but would like to play some role on the international stage in the area of human rights.
Her announcement came amidst speculation in Ireland that she could be offered a top job in the United Nations, such as the commissioner for human rights or refugees.
"It has been a difficult decision for me and I have, with great reluctance, decided not to seek a second term in office," Robinson said in a statement.

"I believe that by the end of this term I will have made my contribution and that the people will give a mandate to a new president with the vision to represent them as we move into the new millennium."
Robinson overcame odds of 1,000-1 in the male-dominated world of Irish politics to win the 1990 presidential election and become the country's first woman head of state.
A lawyer, she injected new vibrancy in the presidency, refusing to follow in the track of earlier incumbents who were rarely seen and never heard.
In her statement, she thanked the people of Ireland for their trust and goodwill during her presidency, which is due to end in December.
"The unwavering support I have received as President has enabled me to contribute to the development of the office as a resource for all the people, one that is open, inclusive and tolerant."
But she said she now had a sense of having made her contribution and believed there should be an opportunity to renew the relationship between president and people.

"I have given what I could and I have lots to do. It's better that I try and do that elsewhere, rather than carry on without having a full sense of the mandate that I had and that I hope I have worked out and will have worked out by the end of the seven years," she told Irish state radio.
Robinson said that she was interested in a role in the area of human rights once her terms ends.
"I have a real commitment, particularly in the area of human rights. I would like to continue in that area and I will be exploring the possibilities of that."
A noted orator, Robinson quickly acquired a high profile internationally during her presidency, espousing a deep concern for human rights and knowledge of Third World development issues.
Last year she was mentioned as a possible replacement for United Nations Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, but the job went to Kofi Annan of Ghana.

Her announcement comes as the U.N.'s first High Commissioner for Human Rights, Jose Ayala Lasso, leaves his post to return to Ecuador to become foreign minister. An interim replacement has been named, but it is considered unlikely that the appointment of a permanent successor would be held up until the end of the year, when Robinson would be available.
Irish Prime Minister John Bruton, informed by telephone of Robinson's decision, said he accepted and respected it and that the government would support Robinson in whatever office she sought.
"In a special way, she has emphasised the role of women in Irish life. She has symbolised the modernisation of Ireland," Bruton said in a statement.

"She has conducted her office in a way that was inclusive of all the people Ireland, especially those who might otherwise be marginalised from the mainstream of political, social and economic decision-making.
"She was, and continues to be, a President for all the people," he said.
